graders.evidence:
**No. After the 2.6.1 upgrade you won't have 30-day webhook replay unless you add an external archive.**

The FluxQueue 2.6.1 docs (published 2026-11-04, [Retries and Replay](https://docs.fluxqueue.dev/2-6-1/retries-and-replay)) say:
- **The dead-letter queue keeps items for 72 hours by default**, and there's **no built-in 30-day replay**. The docs say to archive dead-letter items externally if you need longer retention.
- Retries are now capped at **12 delivery attempts by default**, with exponential backoff that maxes out at 15 minutes. You can change this with `FLUXQUEUE_RETRY_LIMIT` (1–50). Even at 50 attempts, retries only cover about half a day, so raising the limit won't get you near 30 days.

**Why we thought we were covered:** our vault page "FluxQueue webhook retention" (reviewed 2026-07-20, now marked stale) says 2.5 retried with no cap and kept dead-letter items for 30 days, so it concluded we didn't need an external archive. 1. Set up an external dead-letter archive (for example, export failed items to S3 or a database with 30-day retention) and test that you can replay from it, or
2. Hold the upgrade until that's in place.

graders.evidence:
**Don't build the billing service yourself.** Use Stripe Billing's usage-based meters for the monthly invoices. Build one small piece in-house: hard-cap enforcement. No billing vendor, Stripe included, should sit on your request path to decide whether to block a customer.

## Recommended setup

```
events ──► your ingest ──► Redis/DB counter per customer per period ──► allow / reject  (hard cap, in-house)
                                   │
                                   └─► rollup job (e.g. every 1–5 min) ──► Stripe Meter Events ──► monthly invoice
```

**1. Invoicing goes to Stripe meters.** Stripe handles proration, invoice generation, tax, dunning and the customer portal. That work is what usually takes months in a homegrown billing system, and you don't have months.

**2. Send Stripe rolled-up usage, not individual events.** At 150 events/s you're producing about 13M events a day and about 390M a month. Don't forward each one. Total them per customer per minute (or per 5 minutes) and send one meter event per customer per interval with an idempotency key. This keeps you well clear of Stripe's rate limits, makes retries safe, and leaves you with a clean set of numbers to reconcile against.

**3. Build the hard caps yourself.** This is about 1–2 weeks of work:
- Each customer gets an atomic counter keyed by customer and billing period, e.g. Redis `INCRBY` with the cap checked in a Lua script so concurrent requests don't overshoot.
- Store the cap limits in your own database, synced from the Stripe price or plan metadata.
- Decide now what a "hard" cap means: reject at 100%, or allow a small grace margin. Also decide what happens at period rollover and when a customer upgrades mid-period.
- Add a soft warning at around 80% using your own counter. Stripe's billing alerts can work as a backstop notification, but they're too slow to enforce anything.

**4. Reconcile nightly.** Compare your counters with Stripe's meter totals and alert if they drift apart. This is cheap to build and keeps invoices from surprising you or your customers.

## When another option makes sense

- **OpenMeter or Lago** (both open source, self-hostable or cloud) are worth a look if you want caps and entitlements as a ready-made product and expect complicated pricing later, like credits, prepaid commits or tiered overages. They can still sync invoices to Stripe. The cost is another system to run, which is a lot to take on with a January deadline.
- **Orb or Metronome** are a good fit if usage-based pricing is central to your business and you want pricing changes to be configuration, not code. They take longer to set up and cost more than Stripe on its own.

## Timeline

Seven to eight weeks is realistic for Stripe meters plus in-house caps, with a few weeks of buffer. Run one billing cycle in shadow mode during December, generating invoices without charging anyone, so you've checked the numbers before the first real invoice.

## Before you commit

Confirm Stripe's current meter-event rate limits and Billing fees for your volume. Also check whether the event stream itself is what you bill on, or whether you bill on a value derived from it (tokens, GB, and so on). If it's derived, the rollup job has to compute that value.

**My recommendation: buy the invoicing and build the caps.** Stripe Billing Meters can handle the invoicing as is. Hard caps are a small piece of work, but no billing product enforces them reliably in your request path, so you'll need to build that part either way.

## Why this split

**Invoicing: use Stripe Billing Meters.**
- At 150 events/sec you're well within Stripe's meter event ingestion limits, and that's true even before batching.
- Send aggregated usage, not raw events. A per-customer rollup every minute (or every few minutes) works well. It cuts API volume by orders of magnitude, makes retries cheap, and gives you a clean reconciliation point.
- Stripe then handles the hard parts: tiered and volume pricing, proration, invoice generation, tax, dunning, and the customer portal. Building those yourself is where in-house billing projects run late, and you don't have time for that before January.

**Hard caps: build them yourself.**
- Stripe's usage alerts are asynchronous notifications. They can't block a request at the moment a customer hits the limit, and the same is mostly true of the metering vendors.
- What you need is small: an atomic per-customer counter keyed by billing period, such as Redis `INCRBY` plus a check in a Lua script, or a conditional update in your database. Check it on the ingest or API path and return a 429 (or degrade service) when a customer is over their cap.
- Write each customer's cap limit into your own database alongside their plan. Don't call Stripe on the hot path.

## Things that will bite you if you don't plan for them
1. **Two sources of truth.** Your cap counter and Stripe's meter totals will drift. Make the rollup job the only thing that reports usage to Stripe, give each report an idempotency identifier (e.g. `customer:period:minute`), and run a daily reconciliation job.
2. **Billing period alignment.** Caps need to reset at the start of each customer's Stripe billing cycle, not on the calendar month, unless every customer is anchored to the 1st. Deciding this now is much easier than changing it later.
3. **Late and corrected data.** Stripe only accepts meter events with timestamps inside a limited backdating window, and corrections go through meter event adjustments, not by resending events. Design your pipeline so usage gets reported promptly.
4. **Behaviour at the cap.** Decide whether to hard-reject, allow a grace margin, or degrade service, and whether customers get warnings at 80% and 100%. This is a product decision, and it usually takes longer to settle than the code.

## When to use a metering vendor instead
Consider Orb, Metronome, Lago or OpenMeter (the last two are open source and self-hostable) if any of these apply:
- Pricing involves prepaid credits, commitments or drawdowns, or contracts negotiated per customer.
- Finance needs to change pricing without a deploy.

No, not as one shared balance. It can put all of them behind one endpoint, but each provider's quota stays separate.

**What CLIProxyAPI 7.4 does** (per the official docs, [Routing](https://cliproxyapi.dev/docs/7-4/routing) and [Provider Limits](https://cliproxyapi.dev/docs/7-4/provider-limits)):
- **One endpoint and key:** a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and local API key in front of Claude subscription logins, Codex logins and OpenRouter API keys.
- **Account groups:** you can group accounts for each provider, rotate requests across them, and fall back to another account when one hits its limit.

- OpenRouter usage always comes out of that OpenRouter account's prepaid credits.
- Usage doesn't move between providers. Leftover Claude allowance can't pay for Codex requests or become OpenRouter credit.

So the most you get is: when one account or provider runs out, requests go to another one you've set up. Your total capacity is the sum of separate limits that each still run out on their own.

Before routing subscription logins through a proxy, especially if other people share it, check Anthropic's and OpenAI's terms for those subscriptions.
